lectures.title: Acid-Base Part I
lectures.note: Built from the slides plus the lecture recording: the recording only chooses which facts to star, it adds no content. The four simple disorders are the conditions. The slides give no incidence or mortality figures; the only outcome stated is the unsustainable pH (below 6.7 or above 7.6), kept as the slide prints it. The board cases at the end of the lecture are not in the deck and are not used.

conditions.name: Respiratory acidosis
conditions.prof_note: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is the first cause to think of; the sleepy, confused patient; acute versus chronic is read from how far the kidneys have compensated; the obesity hypoventilation syndrome triad is a frequent question.

fields.name: Respiratory acidosis (acute or chronic)
fields.definition: Hypoventilation raising the partial pressure of carbon dioxide (greater than 40 mm Hg) and causing acidemia (pH below 7.35); may be accompanied by hypoxemia; may be acute or chronic
fields.etiology: Acute: airway obstruction; pulmonary disease (pneumonia, asthma, pulmonary edema, aspiration pneumonitis); central nervous system depression (recreational drugs, intracranial catastrophe, intravenous sedation); neuromuscular disorders (myasthenia gravis, Guillain-Barré syndrome); thoracic trauma (pneumothorax, flail chest). Chronic: lung disease ([[★ chronic obstructive pulmonary disease]], interstitial lung disease, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis); neuromuscular disorders (muscular dystrophy, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis); obesity hypoventilation syndrome
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: [[★ Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (Pickwickian syndrome): the triad of obesity, sleep disordered breathing and chronic hypercapnia]]
fields.pathology: Hypercapnia is usually from under-excretion (hypoventilation), not excess production. Compensation is renal: the kidneys excrete acid as ammonium chloride and retain bicarbonate, beginning 6 to 12 hours after onset; complete compensation may take days. Bicarbonate rises about 1 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg rise in carbon dioxide acutely and about 3.5 chronically
fields.clinical: Somnolence, confusion, altered mental status, asterixis, myoclonus. Severe hypercapnia: increased cerebral blood flow, intracranial pressure and cerebrospinal fluid pressure; papilledema may be seen
fields.diagnosis: Low arterial pH, increased carbon dioxide, elevated serum bicarbonate; hypochloremia with chronic acidosis (renal excretion of acid as ammonium chloride). Respiratory disorder: compare the bicarbonate with its expected level to judge acute versus chronic
fields.treatment: Treat the underlying cause. Acute: restore ventilation. Chronic: careful oxygen titration; avoid rapid or aggressive carbon dioxide reduction, which causes posthypercapnic metabolic alkalosis

conditions.name: Respiratory alkalosis
conditions.prof_note: The paper bag "doesn't actually do anything": it is not necessary, does not correct carbon dioxide, may lower oxygen and works as a placebo.

fields.name: Respiratory alkalosis (acute or chronic)
fields.definition: Hyperventilation lowering the partial pressure of carbon dioxide and causing alkalemia (pH above 7.45)
fields.etiology: Central hyperventilation (voluntary or psychogenic, cerebrovascular accident, increased intracranial pressure); hyperventilation from hypoxia (high altitude, severe anemia, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, hypotension); toxic or pharmacologic (salicylates, caffeine, nicotine, catecholamines, thyroxine); pulmonary (pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, mechanical hyperventilation, interstitial lung disease); endocrine (pregnancy, hyperthyroidism); septicemia; heat exposure; hepatic failure
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Hypocapnia is usually from excess excretion (hyperventilation). Initial compensation: cells secrete hydrogen ions in exchange for potassium. Then the kidneys excrete bicarbonate and retain chloride, giving a reduced bicarbonate, hypokalemia and hyperchloremia. Bicarbonate falls about 2 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg fall in carbon dioxide acutely and about 5 chronically
fields.clinical: Light-headedness, anxiety, perioral numbness, paresthesias; in severe cases tetany from low calcium, because a high pH increases calcium binding with albumin
fields.diagnosis: Elevated arterial pH, low carbon dioxide; decreased bicarbonate in chronic respiratory alkalosis
fields.treatment: Treat the underlying cause; hyperventilation is usually self-limited. [[★ Breathing into a paper bag is not necessary: it does not correct carbon dioxide, may decrease oxygen, and works as a placebo]]. Rapid correction of chronic respiratory alkalosis may cause posthypocapnia metabolic acidosis

conditions.name: Metabolic alkalosis
conditions.prof_note: Saline responsive is the common type; compensation rarely takes carbon dioxide above 55 mm Hg; urine chloride splits the two types and blood pressure then sorts the saline-unresponsive causes; licorice is "a unicorn".

fields.name: Metabolic alkalosis (saline responsive or saline unresponsive)
fields.definition: Elevated serum bicarbonate causing alkalemia. Two types: saline responsive (a sign of extracellular volume contraction) and saline unresponsive (elevated bicarbonate with euvolemia or hypervolemia)
fields.etiology: Saline responsive: diuretic therapy, posthypercapnia, loss of hydrochloric acid (vomiting, nasogastric suction), antacids, volume contraction. Saline unresponsive, normotensive: severe potassium depletion, hypoparathyroidism and hypercalcemia. Saline unresponsive, hypertensive: primary aldosteronism, exogenous alkali, mineralocorticoids, licorice
fields.epidemiology: [[★ Saline responsive is the more common type]]
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Compensation is decreased ventilation to retain carbon dioxide, about 0.75 mm Hg per 1 mEq/L rise in bicarbonate; [[★ carbon dioxide is rarely above 55 mm Hg from compensation, so a higher value suggests a concurrent primary respiratory acidosis]]
fields.clinical: No characteristic findings; may have orthostatic hypotension; associated hypokalemia causes weakness and hyporeflexia
fields.diagnosis: Elevated arterial pH and serum bicarbonate; increased carbon dioxide with respiratory compensation; decreased potassium and chloride. [[★ Urine chloride differentiates the types: lower in saline responsive (below 25 mEq/L), higher in saline unresponsive (above 40 mEq/L)]]
fields.treatment: Treat the underlying cause. If saline responsive: isotonic saline to correct the extracellular volume deficit, and discontinue diuretics if present

conditions.name: Metabolic acidosis
conditions.prof_note: "By far the most complex": know the two mnemonics, and commit the Winter formula and the anion gap calculation to memory.

fields.name: Metabolic acidosis (normal anion gap or elevated anion gap)
fields.definition: Reduced serum bicarbonate causing acidemia: acids added (intrinsic or exogenous), acid excretion impaired, or bicarbonate lost. Two types: normal anion gap and elevated anion gap
fields.etiology: Elevated anion gap (MUDPILES): methanol, metformin, uremia, diabetic ketoacidosis, paraldehyde, isoniazid, iron, lactic acidosis, ethylene glycol, salicylates, starvation (metabolic and drug or chemical anions). Normal anion gap (USEDCAR): ureteral diversion, saline infusion, exogenous acid, diarrhea, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, adrenal insufficiency, renal tubular acidosis (loss of bicarbonate, chloride retention, acids)
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Increased acid production or ingestion, loss of bicarbonate, or decreased renal acid excretion. Compensation is increased ventilation to lower carbon dioxide; in severe cases hyperventilation is profound, as Kussmaul respirations (increased tidal volume and tachypnea) in diabetic ketoacidosis. The anion gap is the anions other than chloride and bicarbonate; albumin makes up most of the normal gap
fields.clinical: Mainly the signs and symptoms of the underlying disorder, plus compensatory hyperventilation
fields.diagnosis: Decreased pH, bicarbonate and carbon dioxide; hyperkalemia may be present. [[★ Anion gap = sodium - (chloride + bicarbonate), normal 9 to 15]]: normal gap is hyperchloremic, elevated gap is normochloremic. A normal gap does not exclude acidosis and should not override clinical concern (errors: hypoalbuminemia, hypernatremia or hyponatremia, antibiotics). [[★ Winter formula: expected carbon dioxide = 1.5 x measured bicarbonate + 8, plus or minus 2]]; a higher measured value means an added respiratory acidosis, a possible sign of impending respiratory failure
fields.treatment: Treat the underlying disorder, for both gap types; assess the compensatory response with the Winter formula. A pH below 6.7 may warrant therapy to normalize the pH along with treatment of the cause
fields.mortality: A pH below 6.7 (or above 7.6) is unsustainable: it may cause cardiac hypocontractility or irritability, seizures, cerebral edema and metabolic disturbances

lectures.title: Asthma
lectures.note: Built from the slides plus the lecture recording: the recording only chooses which facts to star, it adds no content. Adult content (12 and older) only; epidemiology numbers and emergency management are context, not tested. Brand names and dosing are left out. Where a slide is loose (high-dose inhaled steroid systemic effects, cromolyn filed under bronchodilators, the pneumococcal age band), the field says so or leaves it out.

conditions.name: Asthma
conditions.prof_note: Classifying severity from a patient description (most severe feature wins), the written action plan and zones, inhaler and spacer technique, and drug classes rather than brands were stressed; epidemiology and emergency care are not tested.

fields.name: Asthma (extrinsic and intrinsic types)
fields.definition: [[★ Chronic inflammatory airway disorder with reversible airflow obstruction]] (some long-standing cases irreversible): recurrent breathlessness and wheezing and difficulty getting air out. Airway hyper-responsiveness is excessive bronchoconstriction to a trigger a normal airway ignores
fields.etiology: Not fully understood: genetic predisposition (polygenic) plus environment. [[★ Atopy]] (raised immunoglobulin E; atopic triad of allergic rhinitis, asthma, atopic dermatitis); obesity (body mass index above 30); early viral infection. Inhaled allergens (dust mites most common), occupational sensitizers, air pollution and passive smoke (controversial)
fields.epidemiology: Any age, peak presentation at 3 years; may go quiet in adolescence and return in adulthood. Statistics were not tested. Severity rarely changes: mild rarely becomes severe, severe is usually severe at onset
fields.risk_factors: Atopy, family history, obesity, occupational exposure. Triggers: allergens, viral infections, aspirin and beta blockers, exercise, cold air, pollution, smoke, stress. Allergen avoidance does not reduce the risk of developing asthma. Death risk: frequent bronchodilator use, no or poorly taken inhaled corticosteroid, previous near-fatal admission
fields.pathology: Bronchoconstriction, airway edema, vascular congestion, mucus plugging; lowers the 1-second volume, its ratio to forced vital capacity, and peak flow. Extrinsic: allergen-triggered, most common. Intrinsic (about 10%): negative skin tests, normal immunoglobulin E, adult onset, usually more severe, nasal polyps, may be aspirin sensitive. Other types: occupational, catamenial, cardiac, exercise-induced, aspirin-sensitive
fields.clinical: Episodic wheeze, dyspnea, chest tightness, cough, sputum; worse at night (peak 3 to 4 in the morning); exam may be normal between exacerbations; extrinsic: swollen nasal mucosa, eczema, nasal polyps. Exacerbation: accessory muscle use, leaning forward; wheeze may disappear in a severe exacerbation
fields.diagnosis: [[★ Spirometry before and after a short-acting bronchodilator]]: reduced 1-second volume and ratio; improvement of 12% or more supports asthma; repeat yearly. Provocation testing if nondiagnostic (not below 65% predicted); exercise challenge; allergy testing; exhaled nitric oxide. Home peak flow: 20% change = poor control. [[★ Severity (12 and older): intermittent, mild, moderate, severe persistent by symptoms, nights, rescue use, activity limit and 1-second volume; most severe feature wins]]
fields.treatment: Trigger avoidance; every patient needs a short-acting beta-2 agonist; [[★ inhaled corticosteroid first-line for persistent asthma]] (spacer, rinse); long-acting beta-2 agonist only with an inhaled steroid; add-ons: leukotriene modifier, cromolyn, tiotropium, theophylline (rarely); monoclonal antibodies by specialists; short systemic steroid course for exacerbations, none long-term unless refractory. Avoid aspirin, non-selective anti-inflammatory drugs and beta blockers. Written action plan with zones; vaccines (caution with intranasal influenza); check compliance and technique first when control is poor
fields.mortality: Death uncommon; declining in affluent countries with widespread use of inhaled corticosteroids. Death risk: frequent bronchodilator use, no or poorly taken inhaled corticosteroid, previous near-fatal admission

fields.name: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis
fields.definition: Hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus species (Aspergillus fumigatus)
fields.etiology: Exposure to Aspergillus in a patient with asthma or cystic fibrosis
fields.epidemiology: Occurs almost exclusively with asthma or cystic fibrosis
fields.risk_factors: Asthma; cystic fibrosis
fields.pathology: Vigorous immunoglobulin E and G antibody response to Aspergillus fumigatus
fields.clinical: Acute asthma symptoms and exacerbations despite good control
fields.diagnosis: Raised immunoglobulin E and G antibodies to Aspergillus fumigatus
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

lectures.title: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
lectures.note: Built from the slides plus the lecture recording: the recording only chooses which facts to star, it adds no content. Both the 2020 four-group (A to D) and the 2023 and 2026 three-group (A, B, E) schemes are on the slides. Where the lecturer said any single exacerbation makes a patient high risk, the slides' definition (2 or more moderate, or 1 leading to hospitalization) is used. Brand names, device brands and dosing are left out.

conditions.name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
conditions.prof_note: The group (symptoms times risk) sets the treatment; know both the 2020 A to D and the current A, B, E schemes; spirometry confirms the diagnosis; the airflow grade, assessment test, dyspnea grade and BODE score are testable calculations.

fields.name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) / chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD)
fields.definition: [[★ Persistent airflow obstruction plus respiratory symptoms]] caused by inhaled particulate exposure in the setting of genetic, developmental and social factors; an umbrella of chronic bronchitis and emphysema. Chronic bronchitis without airflow obstruction is not COPD
fields.etiology: [[★ Tobacco smoke (about 90%)]]; biomass burning (indoor cooking and heating, major in low- and middle-income countries); occupational coal dust, gold mining, welding, fumes; alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (about 3 to 4 per 10,000); sedentary lifestyle
fields.epidemiology: About 6% of Americans; third leading cause of death worldwide (2023); underdiagnosis very common; symptoms begin in midlife
fields.risk_factors: Smoking, biomass smoke, occupational exposures, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (age 45 or under, nonsmoker, basilar emphysema, family history), inactivity
fields.pathology: Chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, protease-antiprotease imbalance. Chronic bronchitis subtype: airway narrowing and mucus plugging. Emphysema subtype: alveolar destruction and loss of elastic recoil; centrilobular upper-lobe in smokers, panlobular lower-lobe in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Air trapping and hyperinflation
fields.clinical: Progressive dyspnea (exertional dyspnea is the early sign), chronic cough, sputum, wheeze. Blue bloater (chronic bronchitis): sputum, rhonchi, cyanosis, edema. Pink puffer (emphysema): thin, pursed lips, barrel chest, distant breath sounds. Cor pulmonale, syncope, falls. Screen for heart disease, lung cancer, osteoporosis, depression, reflux, anemia
fields.diagnosis: [[★ Spirometry before and after a bronchodilator: ratio below 0.70]]; response under 12% = irreversible. Airflow grade by 1-second volume: 1 at 80% or more, 2 at 50 to 79%, 3 at 30 to 49%, 4 below 30%. Assessment test 10 or more or dyspnea grade 2 or more = more symptoms. Low diffusing capacity = emphysema. Alpha-1 antitrypsin level below 11 micromol/L. Blood gas only in severe exacerbations
fields.treatment: [[★ Group sets treatment]]: A one bronchodilator; B long-acting beta agonist plus antimuscarinic; E the same pair, add inhaled steroid if eosinophils 300 or more. Inhaled steroid never alone. Oral steroids for exacerbations only. Smoking cessation with counseling, pulmonary rehabilitation (B and E), yearly influenza and pneumococcal vaccines, albuterol rescue. Long-term oxygen for arterial oxygen under 55 mmHg or saturation below 88%. Exacerbation: bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics if more and purulent sputum, noninvasive ventilation for hypercapnia. Older adults: spacer or soft mist devices, active rehabilitation referral, early palliative care
fields.mortality: BODE index (body mass index, obstruction, dyspnea, exercise) estimates 4-year survival: 0 to 2 points about 80%, 3 to 4 about 67%, 5 to 6 about 57%, 7 to 10 about 18%. Survival benefit: smoking cessation, long-term oxygen, noninvasive ventilation

lectures.title: Respiratory Infections and Vaccines
lectures.lecturer: Robert Bobilin, MS, MPAS, PA-C (guest lecturer)
lectures.note: Built from the slides plus the Zoom recording: the recording only chooses which facts to star, it adds no content. The lecturer said vaccines will not be asked in much detail, the example chest films will not be shown as 'what is it', and he promised exam guidance after the lecture. Brand names and dosing are left out.

conditions.name: Acute bronchitis
conditions.prof_note: His theme: 'diagnostic restraint' - no routine antibiotics, whatever the sputum color or cough duration.

fields.name: Acute bronchitis
fields.definition: A usually self-limited viral infection of the large airways; inflammation and mucus cause cough, sometimes with transient wheeze
fields.etiology: Most uncomplicated episodes are viral; bacterial causes are uncommon. Consider pertussis with paroxysmal cough, post-tussive vomiting, whoop or exposure
fields.epidemiology: Follows cold-like symptoms; cough commonly lasts 2 to 3 weeks and may persist longer
fields.risk_factors: A preceding viral upper respiratory infection; smoke and irritants worsen symptoms
fields.pathology: Inflammation and mucus in the large airways; wheeze depends on the severity of airflow limitation
fields.clinical: Low-grade fever, chills, aches, then cough with mucus, worst in the morning ([[★ green or yellow mucus does not mean bacteria]]); dyspnea, wheeze, chest tightness, throat tickle. Exam: central (substernal) wheeze, rhonchi that clear with cough, chest-wall tenderness; consolidation means think pneumonia
fields.diagnosis: [[★ Clinical diagnosis]]; no routine complete blood count, sputum culture or chest film in uncomplicated cases (a blood count cannot tell viral from bacterial); image when vital signs, focal findings or risk suggest pneumonia; test for pertussis, influenza or COVID-19 when it changes care
fields.treatment: [[★ No routine antibiotics]] (amoxicillin/clavulanate, clindamycin and fluoroquinolones are not default treatments); expectation setting, rest, fluids, avoiding smoke, acetaminophen (avoid duplicate acetaminophen in combination products); no routine opioid cough suppressants or corticosteroids; bronchodilator trial for selected wheezing patients; delayed 'pocket' prescription; return for dyspnea, hemoptysis, persistent fever, hypoxemia or worsening

conditions.name: Community-acquired pneumonia (bacterial)
conditions.prof_note: PSI is the preferred admission tool and CURB-65 is complementary; know the outpatient and inpatient regimens and when to withhold antibiotics.

fields.name: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP)
fields.definition: Acute infection of the lung parenchyma and alveolar sacs, acquired outside the hospital or present early in admission; prior healthcare contact does not exclude it
fields.etiology: [[★ Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common pathogen]]; Haemophilus influenzae, respiratory viruses; atypicals Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae and Legionella (cruises, hot tubs, fountains); Klebsiella, Moraxella, MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus), Pseudomonas
fields.epidemiology: About 24.8 cases per 10,000 adults a year; highest incidence over 65; 15 to 20% hospitalized; influenza and pneumonia together are the 8th leading cause of death
fields.risk_factors: Age (young children, older adults), immunocompromise, sick contacts, alcohol and smoking, aspiration, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and heart disease
fields.pathology: Stages: congestion, red hepatization, gray hepatization, resolution (not hard rules)
fields.clinical: Higher fevers and chills, pleuritic or stabbing chest pain, productive possibly purulent cough, dyspnea and tachypnea; sepsis signs when systemic. Exam: crackles or diminished sounds over one lobe, dullness, egophony (E to A), whispered pectoriloquy, increased tactile fremitus, pleural rub
fields.diagnosis: [[★ Chest radiograph]] (lung ultrasound with expertise); oxygen saturation, vital signs, organ function, sepsis risk; [[★ Pneumonia Severity Index plus judgment for admission; CURB-65 complementary]] (0 to 1 home, 2 hospital, 3 to 5 high severity); cultures only for severe disease, resistance risk or failure; computed tomography for uncertainty or cavitation
fields.treatment: Outpatient, healthy: amoxicillin or doxycycline (macrolide alone only if pneumococcal resistance below 25%). Outpatient with comorbidities: amoxicillin/clavulanate, cefpodoxime or cefuroxime plus azithromycin or doxycycline, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone. Inpatient nonsevere: beta-lactam plus macrolide, or a fluoroquinolone alone. Severe: beta-lactam plus azithromycin or a fluoroquinolone. Minimum 3 days (nonsevere), at least 5 days (severe). No routine steroids in nonsevere disease
fields.mortality: CURB-65 risk of death: under 3% (0 to 1), 9% (2), 15 to 40% (3 to 5). Pneumonia Severity Index class mortality: I 0.1%, II 0.6%, III 0.9%, intravenous 9.3%, V 27.0%

fields.name: Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) and ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP)
fields.definition: HAP develops 48 hours or more after admission and was not incubating on admission; VAP develops more than 48 hours after endotracheal intubation
fields.etiology: Staphylococcus aureus and gram-negative bacilli including Pseudomonas and Enterobacterales; VAP more likely Pseudomonas or multidrug-resistant organisms
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Ventilator circuits contaminated by flora, secretions, hands of healthcare workers, circuit changes, tube biofilm, prior antibiotics
fields.pathology: Colonized secretions are inhaled into the lungs through the endotracheal tube
fields.clinical: A new pneumonia during admission or ventilation
fields.diagnosis: Respiratory cultures; local antibiogram, prior cultures and recent antibiotics; early or late timing alone does not select the regimen
fields.treatment: Antipseudomonal beta-lactam with methicillin-sensitive staphylococcal coverage (piperacillin/tazobactam or cefepime); add vancomycin or linezolid for methicillin-resistant S. aureus risk; a second antipseudomonal class for selected high-risk patients; de-escalate; usually 7 days. VAP prevention: early extubation, hand washing, sterile technique, fewer circuit changes, head of bed elevated, secretion drainage and mouth care
fields.mortality: VAP: higher mortality and prolonged intensive care stay

fields.name: Aspiration pneumonia versus aspiration pneumonitis
fields.definition: Aspiration pneumonia: bacterial infection after aspiration of colonized oropharyngeal material. Pneumonitis: sterile chemical injury, often after gastric aspiration
fields.etiology: Anaerobic oral flora and varied organisms; pneumonitis is chemical, not infectious
fields.epidemiology: Can occur in community or hospital settings; elderly patients with dysphagia
fields.risk_factors: Dysphagia, altered consciousness, impaired airway protection (stroke, seizure)
fields.pathology: Gravity-dependent airspace opacity in a lobar or segmental distribution
fields.clinical: Pneumonitis: abrupt respiratory decline after a witnessed aspiration, fever or leukocytosis possible without infection. Pneumonia: infectious syndrome with an infiltrate; the event may be unwitnessed
fields.diagnosis: Chest film showing a gravity-dependent opacity; reassess persistence for secondary infection or complication
fields.treatment: Pneumonitis: support oxygenation and airway, no prophylactic antibiotics. Pneumonia: the community- or hospital-acquired pneumonia regimen by setting and severity; [[★ anaerobic coverage only for abscess or empyema]]; assess swallowing, oral hygiene, positioning

fields.name: Lung abscess
fields.definition: A cavitating lung infection, often after aspiration, that can become chronic
fields.etiology: Anaerobic oral flora, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, nontuberculous mycobacteria, Staphylococcus aureus including methicillin-resistant strains
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Aspiration
fields.pathology: Infection grows and cavitates, damaging tissue; cavity with an air-fluid level
fields.clinical: Insidious, prolonged (weeks): fever, chills, sweats, cough, purulent foul-smelling sputum, hemoptysis, pleuritic pain, dyspnea, malaise; dullness, whispered pectoriloquy, bronchophony, amphoric breath sounds (like breathing across an open jar)
fields.diagnosis: [[★ Cavitary lesion with an air-fluid level]] on chest film and computed tomography; bronchoscopy for obstruction, unusual pathogens or failure to improve
fields.treatment: Usually begins with antibiotics: intravenous ampicillin/sulbactam then oral amoxicillin/clavulanate, for several weeks; clindamycin reserved (C. difficile risk); pulmonary or infectious disease review for drainage or surgery if large or refractory; chest physiotherapy not essential

conditions.name: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
conditions.prof_note: Know the presentation in HIV, the workup ladder (induced sputum, then lavage), TMP-SMX, the steroid trigger (arterial oxygen below 70) and the prophylaxis threshold.

fields.name: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP), formerly Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia (PCP)
fields.definition: A fungal pneumonia, the most common opportunistic infection in people with HIV (human immunodeficiency virus); treated primarily with antibiotics
fields.etiology: Pneumocystis jirovecii
fields.epidemiology: Falling with prophylaxis and antiretroviral therapy; mortality 10 to 20%; still a major cause of death in acquired immunodeficiency syndrome in the United States
fields.risk_factors: HIV (human immunodeficiency virus); chemotherapy, anti-rejection drugs, long-term steroids, organ transplant, blood cancer
fields.pathology: Interstitial pneumonia
fields.clinical: [[★ Progressive exertional dyspnea (95%) and nonproductive cough (95%)]], fever (over 80%), chest discomfort, weight loss, chills; tachypnea, tachycardia, mild crackles, but up to half have a normal exam
fields.diagnosis: Induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage microscopy or polymerase chain reaction (a negative induced sputum does not exclude; go to lavage); beta-D-glucan supports but is not specific; lactate dehydrogenase nonspecific; HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) test, CD4 (cluster of differentiation 4) count and viral load; film: diffuse bilateral perihilar infiltrates; start therapy while confirming if suspicion is high
fields.treatment: [[★ Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole preferred]] (21 days in HIV); alternatives clindamycin plus primaquine, intravenous pentamidine, atovaquone (mild); check G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) before primaquine or dapsone; [[★ steroids if room-air arterial oxygen below 70 mm Hg]]; prophylaxis for CD4 below 100 (or 100 to 200 with detectable HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) RNA); antiretroviral therapy within about 2 weeks

conditions.name: Histoplasmosis
conditions.prof_note: He said it is 'going to show up on your PANCE'.

fields.name: Histoplasmosis
fields.definition: Infection by the fungus Histoplasma capsulatum
fields.etiology: Inhaled from soil and bird or bat droppings (farming, gardening, chicken coops)
fields.epidemiology: United States: mainly central and eastern states, especially the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys; rare
fields.risk_factors: Soil disruption, bird or bat droppings; late HIV
fields.pathology: Granuloma (some patients show only a granuloma on film)
fields.clinical: High fever, chills, myalgias, nonproductive cough, chest pain, headache 3 to 17 days after exposure; some asymptomatic
fields.diagnosis: Ask about geography, soil and droppings; [[★ urine Histoplasma antigen]], often with serum antigen and antibody; early negative tests do not exclude; cross-reacts with Blastomyces; culture or histopathology for severe or uncertain cases
fields.treatment: Mild acute disease in an immunocompetent adult: often observation; itraconazole for prolonged or progressive illness or higher-risk hosts; specialist-led amphotericin induction for severe or disseminated disease; chronic cavitary disease: azole for at least 12 months

fields.name: Cryptococcosis
fields.definition: Infection by Cryptococcus neoformans or C. gattii after environmental inhalation
fields.etiology: Cryptococcus neoformans, C. gattii
fields.epidemiology: Also occurs without immunocompromise
fields.risk_factors: HIV, transplant, steroids
fields.pathology: Nodules or consolidation
fields.clinical: Cough, fever; can mimic community-acquired pneumonia, tuberculosis or cancer; headache or confusion suggests central nervous system involvement
fields.diagnosis: Serum cryptococcal antigen, respiratory culture or histology; evaluate for central nervous system or disseminated disease, often with a lumbar puncture
fields.treatment: Mild isolated pulmonary: fluconazole, generally 6 to 12 months. Severe, central nervous system or disseminated: liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine induction, then fluconazole; infectious disease consultation; monitor toxicity; counsel adherence

conditions.name: Psittacosis
conditions.prof_note: 'A super common medical boards question', though not common enough to deserve a lot of attention.

fields.name: Psittacosis (parrot fever)
fields.definition: Infection by the obligate intracellular bacterium Chlamydia psittaci
fields.etiology: Chlamydia psittaci from parrots, parakeets, canaries and other birds
fields.epidemiology: Rare, about 200 patients a year; an occupational disease (zoo and pet-shop workers, poultry farmers, ranchers)
fields.risk_factors: Handling sick birds, mouth-to-beak resuscitation; human-to-human spread rare
fields.pathology: Stages: flulike illness with a normal film, mild to moderate pneumonia, severe pneumonia, respiratory failure and septic shock
fields.clinical: Fever and cough (50 to 90%, cough usually dry), chills, malaise, dyspnea, sore throat, epistaxis, severe headache, photophobia; [[★ relative bradycardia]], splenomegaly, Horder spots (rose-spot-like macules on the face), hemolytic anemia
fields.diagnosis: Ask about bird exposure; [[★ respiratory nucleic acid amplification test or polymerase chain reaction]]; paired serology cross-reacts; routine culture does not detect it; film: unilateral lower-lobe dense infiltrate, resolving in about 6 weeks
fields.treatment: [[★ Doxycycline]], promptly, 10 to 14 days after fever resolves; macrolide with infectious disease input if tetracyclines are unsuitable; standard precautions; report to public health; veterinary assessment of birds

fields.name: Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia
fields.definition: An atypical pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae, an organism that lacks a cell wall
fields.etiology: Mycoplasma pneumoniae
fields.epidemiology: School-age children and young adults; household or group outbreaks
fields.risk_factors: Outbreak exposure; alcohol and smoking
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Gradual fever, persistent cough, headache, variable chest findings; severe or extrapulmonary illness can occur
fields.diagnosis: Respiratory nucleic acid amplification test when results change care
fields.treatment: Macrolide or doxycycline (respiratory fluoroquinolone an alternative); [[★ beta-lactams are ineffective: no cell wall]]; doxycycline after macrolide failure; no vaccine

conditions.name: Influenza
conditions.prof_note: Treat high-risk patients promptly, even after 48 hours; know who avoids which antiviral.

fields.name: Influenza
fields.definition: A highly contagious airborne orthomyxovirus infection
fields.etiology: Influenza A (more pathogenic, most human infections), B and C; subtypes by hemagglutinin and neuraminidase; antigenic drift and shift
fields.epidemiology: Fall and winter epidemics, peaking in mid-February; incubation 1 to 4 days
fields.risk_factors: Severe disease: under 5, 65 and older, long-term care, immunocompromise, chronic organ disease, pregnancy and 2 weeks postpartum, severe obesity
fields.pathology: Influenza pneumonia: primary viral or secondary bacterial (pneumococcal or staphylococcal)
fields.clinical: Sudden onset: fever 100 to 104 F, cough, sore throat, myalgias, frontal or retro-orbital headache, severe fatigue, red watery eyes, diarrhea in children; wheezes or rhonchi, tachycardia, dry skin
fields.diagnosis: [[★ Rapid molecular assay or reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction]]; a negative rapid antigen test does not exclude; do not wait for results in hospitalized or high-risk patients; chest film to rule out pneumonia in the elderly or high-risk
fields.treatment: [[★ Oseltamivir preferred]] (hospitalized, severe, high-risk, pregnancy), even after 48 hours; baloxavir single dose within 48 hours but not in pregnancy, breastfeeding, severe immunosuppression or hospitalized patients; avoid inhaled zanamivir in asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; amantadine and rimantadine not recommended; avoid aspirin under 18 (Reye syndrome); annual vaccination
fields.mortality: 3 to 5 million cases and 250,000 to 500,000 deaths worldwide a year (context only)

conditions.name: COVID-19
conditions.prof_note: Stratify severity first; oxygenation decides the pathway.

fields.name: Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19)
fields.definition: Disease caused by SARS-CoV-2 (severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2), from asymptomatic infection to respiratory failure
fields.etiology: The virus, spread mainly by inhaling infectious respiratory particles, especially indoors with poor ventilation
fields.epidemiology: Median incubation about 5 days; 18 to 33% asymptomatic
fields.risk_factors: Age (risk rises substantially above 65), immunocompromise, multiple chronic conditions, lack of current vaccination
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Cough, shortness of breath, fever, myalgia, headache; less often sore throat, anosmia, dysgeusia, anorexia, nausea or diarrhea
fields.diagnosis: [[★ Nucleic acid amplification test (including polymerase chain reaction) most sensitive]]; repeat a negative antigen test after 48 hours (2 tests if symptomatic, 3 if not); imaging for pneumonia and complications; D-dimer alone does not diagnose thrombosis. Severity: mild (no dyspnea, normal film), moderate (abnormal film, saturation 94% or more), severe (below 94%, infiltrates over 50%), critical
fields.treatment: High-risk outpatients without hypoxemia: nirmatrelvir/ritonavir within 5 days (check interactions, renal dosing, hepatic contraindications) or 3-day remdesivir within 7 days; molnupiravir only if these are unsuitable, avoid in pregnancy; no steroids without hypoxemia. Hypoxemic inpatients: dexamethasone, consider remdesivir, baricitinib or tocilizumab for rapid progression, thromboprophylaxis

lectures.title: Mycobacterial Infections, Including Tuberculosis
lectures.lecturer: Robert Bobilin, MS, MPAS, PA-C, Emeritus (guest lecturer)
lectures.deck: 38. Mycobacterial Infections including Tuberculosis - Bobilin - 10-29-2025 SV.pptx
lectures.note: Built from the slides plus the Zoom recording, which only chooses which facts to star. Where the lecturer called fever and night sweats 'pathognomonic', the slide (a list of manifestations) is followed. Epidemiology figures are context only. Dosing is left out.

conditions.name: Tuberculosis (pulmonary and extrapulmonary)
conditions.prof_note: Infection versus disease decides infectiousness, evaluation and treatment; know the 5, 10 and 15 mm cut-offs, 3 sputum specimens, isolation and notification, and the 2 + 4 month regimen.

fields.name: Tuberculosis (TB) disease
fields.definition: A chronic granulomatous disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, usually of the lung but able to reach any organ by hematogenous spread
fields.etiology: Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (M. tuberculosis the principal human pathogen; also M. bovis, M. africanum): acid-fast bacilli with lipid-rich, mycolic-acid walls; slow growing
fields.epidemiology: Leading cause of death from a single infectious agent worldwide; about a quarter of the world infected; in the United States most cases occur in people born outside the country
fields.risk_factors: Exposure: close contact, enclosed poorly ventilated spaces, settings with ongoing transmission, high-incidence areas. [[★ Progression: HIV or major immunosuppression, tumor necrosis factor inhibitors, transplant, prolonged steroids, infection within 2 years, infancy and young childhood]]; also diabetes, chronic kidney disease or dialysis, silicosis, low weight, tobacco and alcohol
fields.pathology: Primary infection contained, or progressive primary disease when containment fails; latent foci reactivate with impaired immunity (secondary tuberculosis); caseation, cavities, miliary dissemination
fields.clinical: Persistent cough, hemoptysis or pleuritic pain, fever and night sweats, weight loss, fatigue; may be mild or absent; exam has limited sensitivity and a normal exam does not exclude it. Extrapulmonary: painless lymph node enlargement, pleural effusion, central nervous system (headache, altered mental status), spine (back pain, vertebral destruction), disseminated disease
fields.diagnosis: Tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay shows infection only. [[★ 3 sputum specimens 8 to 24 hours apart (one early morning): smear, culture, a rapid molecular test, susceptibility testing]]; HIV test; chest film (upper-lobe cavities after primary, hilar adenopathy in primary, miliary nodules); imaging cannot confirm
fields.treatment: [[★ Notify the tuberculosis program; airborne isolation room; N95; source control; end isolation by criteria]]. 2 months of isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, then 4 months of isoniazid and rifampin (ethambutol stops once susceptibility is known), daily directly observed therapy; 17-week rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen from age 12; rifampin resistance needs expert management; monthly monitoring for liver injury, interactions, toxicity
fields.mortality: Preventable and curable; post-tuberculosis bronchiectasis and scarring possible

conditions.name: Latent tuberculosis infection
conditions.prof_note: Asymptomatic and not infectious; exclude disease before treating; know the 5, 10 and 15 mm skin test cut-offs.

fields.name: Latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI)
fields.definition: Infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis without disease: asymptomatic, not infectious, no evidence of disease after clinical evaluation
fields.etiology: Mycobacterium tuberculosis contained by the immune system
fields.epidemiology: About a quarter of the world's population has been infected
fields.risk_factors: Exposure risk; reactivation risk with impaired immunity
fields.pathology: Foci can harbor viable organisms for years and reactivate when immunity falls
fields.clinical: None; chest film usually normal
fields.diagnosis: [[★ Tuberculin skin test thresholds: 5 mm (HIV, recent close contact, transplant, major immunosuppression, imaging of prior tuberculosis), 10 mm (exposure or medical risk, congregate settings, children under 5), 15 mm (no risk factors)]]; measure induration, not erythema, at 48 to 72 hours; the interferon-gamma release assay is preferred after BCG (bacille Calmette-Guerin) vaccination; repeat 8 to 10 weeks after exposure if early tests are negative; neither test separates latent infection from disease
fields.treatment: Exclude disease first; 3HP (weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine for 3 months), 4R (daily rifampin for 4 months) or 3HR (daily isoniazid plus rifampin for 3 months); 6H or 9H when rifamycins are unsuitable; check interactions, pregnancy and source-case resistance

fields.name: Nontuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) lung disease (atypical mycobacterial disease)
fields.definition: Pulmonary or extrapulmonary disease from environmental mycobacteria; a respiratory isolate alone does not prove disease
fields.etiology: Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC, a common cause), M. kansasii, M. abscessus
fields.epidemiology: Most infections come from environmental exposure; person-to-person spread uncommon
fields.risk_factors: Bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, immune dysfunction
fields.pathology: Nodular bronchiectasis or fibrocavitary disease
fields.clinical: Chronic cough and sputum, fatigue, weight loss, reduced appetite, dyspnea or hemoptysis
fields.diagnosis: [[★ All domains: compatible symptoms and imaging, alternatives excluded, usually 2 or more sputum cultures of the same species]] (or one bronchial wash or lavage or a qualifying biopsy); an acid-fast smear cannot tell nontuberculous mycobacteria from tuberculosis
fields.treatment: Macrolide-susceptible MAC (specialist-directed): azithromycin, ethambutol and a rifamycin, at least 12 months after culture conversion; cavitary or severe: daily therapy and initial intravenous amikacin; persistent positive cultures after 6 months or more: inhaled liposomal amikacin; other species susceptibility-guided
